The variational method found the exact lowest energy of H2 in simulation. The run on garnet:mock could not confirm it, because the mock device returns made-up counts.

What I ran: I described H2 at 0.735 angstrom in the STO-3G model as a 2-qubit energy formula. The formula has 5 terms: II, IZ, ZI, ZZ and XX. Nuclear repulsion of 0.71997 hartree is added. The circuit has one adjustable angle. It applies an RY rotation, an X gate and a CNOT. I tried 73 angles from -pi to pi on a simulator and kept the best one. Then I narrowed the search around it. The best angle is theta = -2.918 rad. The energy at that angle is -1.137306 hartree. The exact answer from solving the formula directly is also -1.137306 hartree. The two agree to about 1e-15 hartree, which is far below the 0.0016 hartree that chemists count as chemical accuracy.

The final job ran on garnet:mock as one job with two circuits of 4000 shots each. Job ID: 01a16043-b4d4-7305-85b9-a1bfcd576e36. The first circuit measures in the Z basis and gives the II, IZ, ZI and ZZ terms. The second circuit adds a Hadamard gate on each qubit and gives the XX term. The job completed. The counts were about half 00 and half 11 for both circuits. An ideal device would give 01 about 98.8% of the time in the Z circuit. The mock device returns random counts that do not depend on the circuit. So the measured energy of -0.163 hartree is about 0.97 hartree off and says nothing about chemistry. It only shows that the job pipeline works. A real QPU such as Garnet would give an energy near -1.137 hartree, shifted somewhat by noise. That would cost credits, so I did not run it.

The principle: a quantum computer prepares a trial state, measures the energy, and a classical computer adjusts the circuit to lower it. The variational principle says no trial state can go below the true ground energy. So the lowest value found is the best estimate. This loop finds the molecule's ground-state energy.
